schools.summary: Calvin canvasses the theories for Muth-labben (an enemy captain, Goliath, a musical instrument) and prefers the opening of a well-known song, reading the whole psalm as a prayer; Gill takes 'with my whole heart' as open confession in the public congregation.

Henry finds the title uncertain (Goliath, Nabal, or Absalom) and inclines to a mere tune or instrument, the foes being the Philistines; Spurgeon hears a holy resolve to praise God alone, 'half heart is no heart.'
Clarke heaps up the versions - Chaldee 'death of the strong man' (Goliath), Vulgate/LXX 'secrets of the Son,' Houbigant's 'alamoth' (hidden things) - and declines to follow the endless conjectures.

Keil and Delitzsch set Ps 9 as the sequel to Ps 8 and dismiss the title-guesses as 'curious conceits' from a false word-division; Ellicott notes the acrostic begins in its completest form, every clause of the first stanza opening with Aleph.
Augustine takes 'the hidden things of the Son' of the only-begotten Son of God, since 'the Son' named absolutely gives him to be understood.

sides.position: the death of an enemy - Goliath (Chaldee) or Nabal (a transposition of 'labben')
only a musical tune or instrument, or the opening of a known song, to which the psalm was set
'the hidden things of the Son' - a mystical, Christological title

outliers.note: Reads the whole title of the only-begotten Son of God, interpreting 'the hidden things of the Son' Christologically where the rest treat it as a historical or musical superscription.

themes: the psalm as prayer, not mere victory-song

schools.summary: Gill fixes the joy not on self or second causes (horses, chariots, armies) but on the Lord as covenant God, noting the Chaldee's 'in thy Word' and a joy unspeakable and full of glory.
Henry makes it a rule that joy must terminate in God only, not the gift but the Giver; holy joy is the life of thankful praise, fitly sung in psalms, giving glory to the Most High.
Clarke keeps it warm and personal: glad that God has heard and shown mercy, rejoicing in having him as a portion dwelling and working in the heart.
Keil and Delitzsch tie the verse to the next by a preposition of both time and reason (recedentibus hostibus meis retro), the song rising out of the enemy's rout.

themes: joy in the Giver, not the gift
sing to thy name, O Most High

schools.summary: Gill widens the turning-back from the fleeing Philistines to the officers who fell backward at Christ, and to sin, Satan, the world, and antichrist retreating before the Lord's people; they perish as wax melts before fire.
Ellicott renders 'in the turning of mine enemies back' (when or because), and 'fall' as 'stumble through weakness,' the LXX 'are weak'; vv.2-3 form one sentence.
Clarke turns it inward: it is a sure sign of a nearly won conquest over sin when, by resistance, it begins to lose its power - the time to follow on to know the Lord.
Henry: the almighty power of God the enemy cannot withstand; their retreat is their ruin, fulfilled when Jesus' 'I am he' made his enemies fall backward.

themes: fall and perish at thy presence

schools.summary: Gill reads a righteous cause pleaded and established, God by the enemy's fall making plain that David's cause was good.

Ellicott renders 'thou hast made my judgment' (LXX/Vulg) and cites Shakespeare's 'there sits a Judge that no king can corrupt'; Keil and Delitzsch mark the gimel strophe (perhaps carrying daleth and he) and read the act as the sum of many.
Henry gives the throne full weight - God decides controversies, avenges the injured, judges according to truth; present irregularities strengthen belief in the judgment to come.

themes: the gimel strophe of the acrostic

schools.summary: Gill takes the heathen for the Philistines or Amalek, but refers the rebuke chiefly to gospel times and the latter-day extirpation of the antichristian powers.
Clarke reads the destroyed Canaanite nations and presses 'for ever and ever' (leolam vaed) as proof that olam bears its endless sense - where are the Hivites and Jebusites now?
Ellicott sharpens 'put out' to 'blotted out,' the name erased from the civil register (Ps. 69:28; 109:13), and notes the missing Daleth stanza in the acrostic.
Henry reads three ordered strokes - checked (a warning to prevent destruction), cut off, then buried in oblivion and perpetual infamy, the name blotted out.
Gill keeps the vocative address but, passing over Goliath and the Jewish glosses on Esau and Amalek, fixes it on antichrist, the great enemy of Christ and his church.

Henry allows both 'Thou, O enemy, hast destroyed our cities' and 'Thou, O God, hast destroyed their cities,' pressing that the ruin is just, total, and final, the saints looking for a city with stronger foundations.

Ellicott refuses the vocative as unintelligible and renders 'As for the enemy, they are made an utter wreck,' with LXX/Vulg 'with a sound' for the memorial (Sodom, Nineveh, Babylon); Keil and Delitzsch read the strophe as the contrast on which the next verse turns.
Clarke agrees with the correction - 'the enemy is desolated for ever... their memory is perished' - recalling Canaanite cities of which neither name nor vestige remains.

debates.question: How should 'O thou enemy' be read?

sides.position: a vocative directly addressing the enemy - 'O thou enemy, destructions are come to a perpetual end'
the vocative is unintelligible; render 'As for the enemy, they are made an utter wreck and perpetual ruin'

schools.summary: Gill renders 'the Lord shall sit for ever' in rest and quiet, of God's unchangeableness and power, and applies the Chaldee's 'Word of the Lord' to Christ at God's right hand.
Wesley: though cities and people perish, the Lord abides for ever - sufficient for the terror of his enemies and the comfort of his church.
Ellicott reads 'Jehovah sits enthroned for ever,' parallel to 'for judgment has erected his throne.'

Henry comforts himself with God's eternity, sovereignty, and righteousness, sitting unshaken upon the floods (Ps. 29:10); Spurgeon hears the swiftness of divine justice - 'term-time lasts all the year round in the court of King's Bench above.'

themes: the Lord shall endure for ever

schools.summary: Gill notes 'world' is a general name for all the habitable earth, so a universal judgment is meant, finished with the utmost righteousness - the righteous judgment of God.
Ellicott stresses the emphatic pronoun 'he it is who shall minister judgment'; Keil and Delitzsch widen the recent act into a final, comprehensive, impartial judgment of the nations.
Clarke: all the dispensations of God's providence are founded in righteousness and truth.

Henry: God judges by unalterable rules of equity, no colour of exception against his sentence; Spurgeon turns the impartial tribunal into a check against sin and a comfort under slander - no respect of persons with the Holy One of Israel.
Gill reads the oppressed as God's weak and trampled people, and (via the Chaldee's 'Word') makes Christ the refuge typified by the cities of refuge - a strong tower when all else fails.

Ellicott renders 'refuge' as 'a stronghold,' 'oppressed' as 'crushed,' and 'trouble' as being cut off from provisions or water (cf. Jer. 14:1 'drought'); Keil and Delitzsch: a high steep place familiar to David, the crushed one wholly broken in pieces.

Henry: God's people are oppressed and have troublous times appointed, yet may flee to him by faith so no real hurt is done; Spurgeon sets the two halves side by side - the Judge of the wicked is the refuge-city of his saints.
Gill takes the name known as God gracious in the gospel and Christ the all-sufficient Saviour, known affectionately, spiritually, and experimentally, not merely notionally.

Clarke: those with an experimental acquaintance of God's mercy trust him, sure he never forsakes; Wesley glosses the name as God's power, wisdom, faithfulness, and goodness, grounded on the experience of all ages.
Ellicott reads the name as a watchword of strength and 'seek' as to frequent a place (the temple courts); Keil and Delitzsch hear a missionary idea - salvation proclaimed from Zion to all the world.
Henry's graded certainty: the better God is known the more he is trusted (Job 35:14; 2 Chron. 20:12), the more trusted the more sought, and he never disowns those who seek him.

themes: they that know thy name will trust
thou hast not forsaken them that seek thee
salvation from Zion to the world

schools.summary: Gill: 'sing praises' means a modulation of the voice in musical notes (the word used of birds' singing), a work for the saints jointly, as Paul and Silas in prison.

Henry: as heaven is the residence of God's glory, Zion (the church) is the residence of his grace; David commands his subjects and courts his neighbours to sing to the God of Israel, not their false gods.

Clarke makes 'declare his doings' the duty of all the saved, lamenting that Christians so seldom speak of God - because they have nothing to say; Wesley reads 'the people' as the heathen nations and Zion as God's gracious presence.

themes: sing praises to the Lord in Zion
declare his doings among the people

schools.summary: Gill takes the searching as God's own - he knows where the blood of his saints lies, as Abel's, and requires it at the hand of him who shed it, especially the martyrs' blood.

Ellicott renders 'the seeker of bloods,' the goel or avenger of blood, and puts the verbs in the past; Keil and Delitzsch read the strophe as the recollection of the humble crying to God before the deliverance.
Clarke widens the inquisition to all nations who wage destructive wars for wealth or empire; Wesley: the blood of God's holy ones, unregarded for a season, will be severely accounted for.
Henry sets the day of inquisition against the great judgment - God remembers every drop and returns it sevenfold (Deut. 32:43), the cry of the humble sealed among his treasures.
Gill: even a man already shown mercy needs fresh discoveries of it, and flees not to the creature but to God, pleading not merit but mercy.

Henry hears David plead mercy 'having misery only, and no merit,' and 'thou that liftest me up from the gates of death'; Spurgeon calls the petition 'a little prayer-book,' the soul and marrow of prayer, and quotes Trapp on God's 'dead lift.'
Clarke reads the gates of death as an open grave leading to hell, and the gates of the daughter of Zion as the ordinances that help the soul toward heaven.
Keil and Delitzsch note the resolved, tremulous form of 'have mercy' and the vocative 'thou that liftest me up,' taking the gates of death for the gates of the realm of the dead.
Gill: 'all thy praise' is all the acts of divine goodness he had known, too many to reckon up in the present state, yet to be published as far as experience reached.
Henry draws the motive - saved not for his own credit but that God may have the glory - and reads the salvation as typical of the great salvation by the Son of David.
Wesley: the gates are the great assemblies, opposed to the gates of death; 'daughter of Zion' names the people, cities being mothers and their peoples daughters (Egypt, Edom).
Keil and Delitzsch read the church's confidence that it will yet praise God in Zion's gates, rescued from the death its enemies wished, rejoicing in his salvation.

themes: the gates of the daughter of Zion
salvation typical of the Son of David

schools.summary: Gill takes this scene for 'the praise' he vowed - the hunter's pit turned on its digger - reading it prophetically of the nations that join antichrist and are ruined by their own design against Christ's kingdom.
Ellicott refers the figure to Ps. 7:16; Keil and Delitzsch fix the Hebrew verb 'to sink in,' the wicked pressed into the net they hid, their own foot caught.
Clarke points back to his note on Ps. 7:15 - the covered pit disguised with reeds, the plotter undone by his own scheme.

Henry: God shames the wicked with an inglorious fall (Ps. 7:15), providence ordering that persecutors are ruined by their own projects (drunkards kill themselves, the contentious bring mischief on themselves); Spurgeon bids the reader pause and meditate, the snare snaring its own maker.

themes: sunk in the pit they made
the foot taken in the net
Higgaion and the call to pause

schools.summary: Gill reads the judgment on antichrist as the means of making God's name and perfections known in all the earth, a just retaliation repaying the persecutor in his own coin.

Ellicott renders 'Jehovah hath made himself known... snaring the wicked in the work of his own hands,' and holds Higgaion's sense open (meditation, Ps. 19:14; solemn sound, Ps. 92:3); Keil and Delitzsch hear the retrospect pass into a guaranteed future.
Clarke reads 'Higgaion, Selah' as 'Meditate on this; mark it well,' allowing also a musical direction like Presto or Largo; Wesley calls it a musical term or a note of attention for deep meditation.
Henry takes Higgaion as a note extraordinary commanding special regard, both present judgments and the judgment to come to be meditated upon.

debates.question: Is 'Higgaion' a call to meditate or a musical direction?

sides.position: a note of meditation or attention - 'mark it well'
a direction to the musicians - a change in the music or 'solemn sound'

themes: the Lord is known by his judgments
the wicked snared in his own work

schools.summary: Gill notes the 'return to the grave' rendering but, since that is common to the righteous, takes it of hell, the place of torment, where the beast and false prophet are cast into the lake of fire.
Clarke keeps and heightens 'headlong into hell, down into hell' (lisholah very emphatic); Wesley glosses the forgetting of God as not regarding his precepts or threatenings.

Ellicott calls 'turned into hell' 'a most unfortunate rendering' and argues for 'return to the grave'/dust (Gen. 3:19; Job 30:23), the verbs perhaps imperative; Keil and Delitzsch read the redactio in pulverem, man returning to dust.

Henry hears the wicked turned into hell as captives to a prison-house, forgetfulness the root of all wickedness; Spurgeon warns that the forgetters of God, not only the profane, share the nethermost hell.

debates.question: Does the verse consign the wicked to hell, or return them to the grave and dust?

sides.position: to hell, the place of torment - 'headlong into hell'
to the grave, the dust, and the world of the dead - 'shall return to the grave'

themes: the wicked shall be turned into hell

schools.summary: Gill: God's needy people, strictly never forgotten (engraven on his hands), may yet seem forgotten and lie long under affliction while the holy city is trodden under foot.

Ellicott marks the emphatic negative ruling both clauses (Ps. 35:19) and 'the expectation of the poor' as the hope of being righted; Keil and Delitzsch read the confident turn from judgment witnessed to deliverance to come.
Clarke: the needy, whose expectation is from the Lord, are never finally forgotten, though deliverance be delayed for the greater confusion of enemies and manifestation of mercy.

Henry: God's people, thinking themselves forgotten, must wait, for the vision is for an appointed time and he cannot forget them though a woman forget her sucking child; Spurgeon answers Satan's lie that their hope shall perish - they wait, but not in vain.

themes: the expectation of the poor shall not perish

schools.summary: Gill reads 'Arise, O Lord' as a call for God to rise to the destruction of his enemies and the salvation of his people.

Ellicott sharpens 'let not mere man be defiant'; Keil and Delitzsch trace 'Arise, O Lord' to Moses (Num. 10:35) and correct 'let not man become strong' to 'let him not act as though possessed of power.'
Clarke prays that this may be the time God will deliver his poor people under oppression and persecution.

Henry: 'Shall mortal man be too hard for God, too strong for his Maker?' - restrain them and let the heathen be judged in thy sight; Spurgeon calls prayers the believer's weapons, faith giving the signal 'Arise, O Lord.'

themes: let mere man not be defiant
the heathen judged in thy sight

schools.summary: Gill reads a bold, fearless generation and prays God to inject fear into them, as at the overthrow of Babylon when her kings and merchants stand afar off for fear of her torment.

Henry: God can make the stoutest tremble and flee when none pursues, to own they are but men - weak, mutable, mortal, accountable; Spurgeon marvels that crowns, learning, and the wealth of Croesus leave their owner but a man.

Clarke parts from the received text: LXX/Vulg/Syriac read 'place a lawgiver or teacher over them' (Coverdale, 'set a Schoolmaster over them'), the reading of all versions but the Chaldee, though some MSS read morre 'fear'; he marks Selah as 'mark well' and records Horsley's threefold division of the psalm.
Ellicott confirms the difficulty - the versions 'place a lawgiver or master over them,' Hitzig 'set a guard upon them,' the present reading 'put a terror upon them.'

debates.question: Does the verse read 'put them in fear' or 'set a teacher/lawgiver over them'?

sides.position: 'put them in fear' / a terror upon them - the received Hebrew reading
'place a lawgiver or teacher over them' - with the LXX, Vulgate, Syriac, and Coverdale

themes: know themselves to be but men
